Transparent photovoltaic (TPV) devices have the potential to revolutionize
photovoltaic (PV) technology by enabling on-site generation while minimizing
visual impact. However, a major challenge in the development of TPV, as well as
for many PV technologies, is the open-circuit voltage (Voc) deﬁcit, which limits
their efﬁciency. In this work, the development of wide-bandgap inorganic-based
TPV devices is reported with a focus on low-cost, earth-abundant, stable, and
nontoxic materials. The device structure consists of an ultrathin hydrogenated
amorphous silicon (a-Si:H) absorber and metal-oxide layers as selective contacts.
Herein, novel approach is presented to signiﬁcantly improve device performance,
especially in Voc, by introducing molecular dipoles in the device electron-transport
layer. By incorporating polyethyleneimine or poly(amidoamine) G1 and G2
dipoles, Voc (from 410 mV up to 638 mV) is signiﬁcantly increased without
sacriﬁcing the average photopic transmittance of the device, leading to a record
efﬁciency for this particular approach in TPV. Measurements conﬁrm excellent
long-term stability. This approach can potentially allow tuning the work function
of the selective contacts enabling the use of low-cost, earth-abundant materials
that are not optimized for a particular absorber. Furthermore, this solution
circumvents the issue of low Voc by a simple interface treatment.

The integration of dipoles[12] has been explored in organic
electronic devices, such as organic solar cells,[13,14] organic
light-emitting diodes and ferroelectric materials,[15] to enhance
carrier injection, and improve charge-carrier mobility.[16] In solar
cells and other electronic devices, careful incorporation of dipoles
through material selection, deposition techniques, and device
engineering optimizes their performance.[17] Different research
works have evidenced that they serve as passivation layers on
solar cell surfaces, reducing charge carrier recombination and
improving efﬁciency.[18,19] Furthermore, they facilitate charge
separation in solar cells, leading to more efﬁcient charge extrac-
tion and power generation. Ongoing research continues to
explore innovative ways to integrate dipoles, pushing the bound-
aries of efﬁciency and performance further in these devices. As
for inorganic solar cells, there has been less research on the
matter, although it seems a very promising approach in order
for photovoltaic (PV) devices to meet their theoretical limits
and maximize PCE especially by maximizing their open-circuit
voltage (Voc).
In this work, different molecular dipoles have been imple-
mented into device architectures, speciﬁcally at the electron-
transport layer (ETL)/absorber interfaces of a-Si:H/oxide TPV
devices. These devices have been characterized and compared
against a reference structure without the interfacial dipoles.
The reference device architecture consists of soda lime glass
(SLG)/ﬂuorine-doped tin oxide (FTO)/aluminum-doped zinc
oxide (AZO)/ZnO/a-Si:H/V2O5/AZO and the studied devices
incorporate molecular dipoles embedded as an interfacial nano-
metric ﬁlm between the AZO and ZnO ﬁlms. TPV characteriza-
tion of these devices has been carried out. Speciﬁcally, the
temperature-dependent Voc characteristics have been studied
and suggest that the Voc improvement can be correlated to the
dipolar moment of the interfacial layer at the electron-selective
contact. Additionally, scanning transmission electron microscopy
and energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (STEM–EDX) measure-
ments have been carried out. Optical characterization has con-
ﬁrmed
the
high
transparency
of
devices
and
that
the
incorporation of interfacial dipoles has negligible effect on the
optical characteristics of the devices. This research is potentially
relevant for the advancement of thin-ﬁlm TPV technologies as well
as for conventional PV technologies, and other technologies in
general that rely on advanced CTL/active layer/CTL architectures.
2. Results and Discussion
Planar ultrathin TPV devices are fabricated with the following
architecture: SLG/FTO/ETL/a-Si:H/V2O5/AZO. The most inno-
vative focus of this study consists in the introduction of molecu-
lar dipoles at the ETL. A reference device is prepared using an
ETL composed of AZO/ZnO and in parallel samples are fabri-
cated intercalating molecular dipoles AZO/dipole/ZnO. Three
different molecules are studied: a branched conjugated polymer,
polyethyleneimine (PEI), and two different generations (G1, G2)
of the dendrimeric macromolecule poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM)
(Figure 1). For the different samples, AZO, ZnO, and V2O5 ﬁlms
have been deposited in parallel in a single process to be able to
make accurate comparisons focusing on the effect of the dipolar
molecule incorporation. In this case, a 30 nm a-Si:H ﬁlm

We begin by analyzing the optical properties of the completed

2.1. Optical Characterization and Current Density–Voltage and
Voc–T Characteristics of TPV Devices
In this section, the complete device structure is characterized
by measuring their reﬂectance and transmittance by optical spec-
trophotometry. The complete devices were fabricated with the
same conditions using different dipole layers in the architecture
including PEI and dendrimer PAMAM Generation 1 (G1) and
Generation 2 (G2) leaving the rest of the structure unchanged.
The measurement allows the determination of the transmittance
spectra of complete TPV devices, which will serve as input for
calculation of average photopic transmittance (APT) and color
rendering index (CRI).
The optical measurements of reﬂectance and transmittance
for the completed devices were conducted in the wavelength
range of 300–800 nm as depicted in Figure 2. These spectra were
employed to determine the values of APT and CRI, as per the
equations provided in the methodology outlined by Traverse
et al.[20] All these parameters are summarized in Table 1.
From the transmittance measurements, it has been possible
to calculate the CIE color coordinates. The coordinates as well
as the CIE color maps are provided in Figure S7, Supporting
Information. As a standard in TPV characterization, from optical
measurements and external quantum efﬁciency (EQE) measure-
ments, we provide the photon balance check graphs in Figure S8,
Supporting Information. These measurements conﬁrm no over-
estimation of generated photocurrent.

Spectral response measurements were performed on the differ-

4. Experimental Section
Sample Preparation: Transparent solar cells (fabricated in this work
present the structure SLG/FTO/AZO/(dipole)/ZnO/a-Si:H/V2O5/AZO.
Commercial SLG/FTO substrates (Merck; Rsh = 10 Ω sq1) were used
as substrate and transparent back-contact. Prior to deposition, substrates
were rinsed in distilled water, dried in Ar ﬂux and afterward cleaned by
subsequent 10 min ultrasonic baths in isopropanol and ultrapure H2O
at room temperature, followed by a drying step in Ar ﬂux and concluding
with a 5 min O3 treatment. A 75 nm AZO ﬁlm was grown in an ALD system
(Savannah S200, Cambridge Nanotech) at 135 °C, using precursors dieth-
ylzinc (DEZ 95%, STREM), ultrapure H2O, and trimethylaluminum (TMA
99%, STREM) and using N2 as purging gas. A total of 21 supercycles at a
19:1 DEZ:TMA ratio were performed, with 19 H2O/N2/DEZ/N2 (20 ms/
3 s/15 ms/3 s) cycles and 1 H2O/N2/TMA/N2 (50 ms/1 s/20 ms/5 s)
cycle. After the AZO deposition, the dipolar molecules studied were depos-
ited on top (except for the reference device, without any dipolar ﬁlm). For
the PEI ﬁlm, fresh solutions of PEI (Merck; 20%) dissolved in methanol
(0.01 wt%) were spin coated at 5000 rpm for 50 s and immediately after
were transferred to a hot plate at 90 °C to remove any solvent. This method
yielded a 2 nm ﬁlm. For the PAMAM ﬁlms, fresh solutions of PAMAM
(Merck;
20 wt%)
were
prepared
dissolving
PAMAM
in
methanol
(0.01 wt%). This was done identically for both G1- and G2-PAMAM.
These solutions were spin coated at 5000 rpm for 50 s and immediately
transferred to a hot plate at 90 °C to remove any solvent. The following
step consisted in depositing an interfacial ZnO ﬁlm of 8 nm, which helped
making a better contact with the absorber/ETL and also served as a cap-
ping or protection layer so that the dipolar ﬁlms were not degraded in the
heat and plasma that the ﬁlms would see in the plasma enhanced chemical
vapor deposition (PE-CVD) of a-Si:H. Afterward, intrinsic a-Si:H ultrathin
ﬁlms of 30 nm were deposited by PE-CVD (Elettrorava) with a radio fre-
quency power supply of 13.56 MHz at 6 W. Substrate temperature was
measured at 220–250 °C during deposition, with a mixed 36/12 sccm
SiH4/CH4 atmosphere and with deposition time of 4 min, respectively.
To ﬁnish the solar cells, the HTL and front contact were deposited in a
single sequential ALD process without breaking vacuum. V2O5 was grown
at 165 °C, using tetrakis(ethylmethylamino)-vanadium (IV) (C12H32N4V)
(TEMAV 99%, STREM) and ultrapure H2O using again N2 as carrier
and purging gas. Immediately after 125 supercycles H2O/N2/TEMAV/
N2 (2 s/3 s/3 s/3 s), without breaking vacuum and keeping T = 165 °C,
AZO was deposited at a 19:1 ratio for 75 supercycles. Once the sample
was fully grown, the active area cells were isolated using a photolitho-
graphic process followed by a wet chemical etching process that effectively
isolated the cells from each other. First, photoresist at room temperature
was spread on the surface of the samples and was statically spin coating
for 30 s at 30.000 rpm. Immediately after, it was taken to a furnace at
105 °C for 20 min to evaporate the residual solvent. Then, UV photolithog-
raphy was performed with a positive mask with square patterns deﬁning a
cell active area of 0.20 cm2. Afterward, a two-step etching process was per-
formed. The ﬁrst stage used HCl at 10% to remove the AZO/V2O5 layer.
The ﬁnal etching used an isotropic etching solution of HF þ HNO3 to
attack and remove the rest of the stack (a-Si:H/ZnO/dipole/AZO) down
to the FTO, which remained unaffected. As a result, the active area pro-
tected with the resin would remain and the subcells would be effectively
isolated from each other allowing for J–V characterization without the need
of a mask.
Characterization: Spectrophotometry measurements were carried out
with a UV–vis–NIR spectrophotometer (Perkin Elmer Lambda L950) with
an integrating sphere, in single-beam conﬁguration, in transmittance and
reﬂectance mode with spectral range from 300 to 800 nm to measure the
completed device total transmittance and reﬂectance. This data was also
used to calculate the device APT, CRI, and CIE color coordinates and color
map. J–V measurements under illumination were carried out using an AAA
class solar simulator with AM1.5G illumination calibrated using an
National Renewable Energy Laboratory-certiﬁed Si reference solar cell
(Abet Technologies Model 15 150). Electrical measurements were carried
out with a source-measure unit (Keithley SMU 2400) in four-wire sense
mode, remotely controlled by the software Tracer (ReRa solutions) using
an IEEE 488 GPIB instrument control device (National Instruments GPIB-
USB-HS). Voc–T measurements were carried out in the same manner.
Temperature was controlled using a Linkam system and measurements
were carried out from 300 K down to 100 K in temperature intervals of
25 K. Spectral response measurements were acquired using a spectral
response
system
(Bentham
PVE300)
calibrated
with
Si
and
Ge
photodiodes. For optoelectronic measurements the samples were placed
in a dark opaque matt to avoid any back-reﬂections that could alter the
characterization of the transparent solar cells.

measured at 220–250 °C during deposition, with a mixed 36/12 sccm
SiH4/CH4 atmosphere and with deposition time of 4 min, respectively.
To ﬁnish the solar cells, the HTL and front contact were deposited in a
single sequential ALD process without breaking vacuum. V2O5 was grown
at 165 °C, using tetrakis(ethylmethylamino)-vanadium (IV) (C12H32N4V)
(TEMAV 99%, STREM) and ultrapure H2O using again N2 as carrier
and purging gas. Immediately after 125 supercycles H2O/N2/TEMAV/
N2 (2 s/3 s/3 s/3 s), without breaking vacuum and keeping T = 165 °C,
AZO was deposited at a 19:1 ratio for 75 supercycles. Once the sample
was fully grown, the active area cells were isolated using a photolitho-
graphic process followed by a wet chemical etching process that effectively
isolated the cells from each other. First, photoresist at room temperature
was spread on the surface of the samples and was statically spin coating
for 30 s at 30.000 rpm. Immediately after, it was taken to a furnace at
105 °C for 20 min to evaporate the residual solvent. Then, UV photolithog-
raphy was performed with a positive mask with square patterns deﬁning a
cell active area of 0.20 cm2. Afterward, a two-step etching process was per-
formed. The ﬁrst stage used HCl at 10% to remove the AZO/V2O5 layer.
The ﬁnal etching used an isotropic etching solution of HF þ HNO3 to
attack and remove the rest of the stack (a-Si:H/ZnO/dipole/AZO) down
to the FTO, which remained unaffected. As a result, the active area pro-
tected with the resin would remain and the subcells would be effectively
isolated from each other allowing for J–V characterization without the need
of a mask.
Characterization: Spectrophotometry measurements were carried out
with a UV–vis–NIR spectrophotometer (Perkin Elmer Lambda L950) with
an integrating sphere, in single-beam conﬁguration, in transmittance and
reﬂectance mode with spectral range from 300 to 800 nm to measure the
completed device total transmittance and reﬂectance. This data was also
used to calculate the device APT, CRI, and CIE color coordinates and color
map. J–V measurements under illumination were carried out using an AAA
class solar simulator with AM1.5G illumination calibrated using an
National Renewable Energy Laboratory-certiﬁed Si reference solar cell
(Abet Technologies Model 15 150). Electrical measurements were carried
out with a source-measure unit (Keithley SMU 2400) in four-wire sense
mode, remotely controlled by the software Tracer (ReRa solutions) using
an IEEE 488 GPIB instrument control device (National Instruments GPIB-
USB-HS). Voc–T measurements were carried out in the same manner.
Temperature was controlled using a Linkam system and measurements
were carried out from 300 K down to 100 K in temperature intervals of
25 K. Spectral response measurements were acquired using a spectral
response system (Bentham PVE300) calibrated with Si and Ge
photodiodes. For optoelectronic measurements the samples were placed
in a dark opaque matt to avoid any back-reﬂections that could alter the
characterization of the transparent solar cells.
